solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lake circled by hungry tailless bird

indicators.note: something circled is ringed round, so one piece sits inside another
without a tail means the final letter of a word is dropped

blocks.note: keen or avid is EAGER, docked of its last letter
the standard map abbreviation for a lake

explanation.surface: A hungry bird with no tail wheels around over a lake, hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: EAGE takes L between its G and final E to give EAGLE. The surface bird is the definition too, so the solver hunts for a second bird that is not there.
explanation.definitionFit: The eagle is a large bird of prey, a straightforward example of the category.

clue.text: Cross with journalists after European editor spoke

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for European
a cross is the letter X in shape
the press are journalists collectively
standard abbreviation for an editor

explanation.surface: A European editor, angry with the journalists, spoke out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like the adjective angry, but it is the letter X, drawn as a cross; 'after' puts the journalists behind that X.
explanation.definitionFit: To have expressed a view is to have voiced or stated it, so the past tense matches.

clue.text: Good arguments for sprouts

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for good
rows (rhyming with cows) are noisy quarrels

explanation.surface: Someone makes a good case for eating Brussels sprouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprouts' reads as the vegetable but is the verb: a plant that sprouts is getting bigger.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that sprouts is shooting up and developing, a synonym in the verb sense.

clue.text: Plain I’ve got over depression

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting something over turns it upside down, so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: the contraction taken letter by letter
a dent is a small hollow or depression in a surface

explanation.surface: Someone says they have plainly recovered from a bout of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low mood, but it is a physical dent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something plain is obvious and clear to see, which is what evident describes.

clue.text: Feeling wicked, cutting nearly everyone off

indicators.note: almost all of a word means its final letter goes
cutting something off removes it from the word it was attached to

blocks.note: British slang, wicked means brilliant or fantastic
everyone is ALL, trimmed of its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone feels wicked, cutting nearly everyone out of their life.
explanation.walkthrough: SENSATIONAL loses AL from its end to leave SENSATION. 'Wicked' as praise is British youth slang, meaning excellent rather than evil.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a physical feeling or perception, such as a tingling in the hand.

clue.text: Dirk could be inside this studio initially with Ted?

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: first letter of the word
Ted Heath was the British Conservative prime minister of 1970 to 1974

explanation.surface: Could the actor Dirk (Bogarde) be in the studio with Ted?
explanation.walkthrough: Dirk reads as a first name, like Dirk Bogarde, but it is a Scottish dagger. Ted Heath was a British prime minister in the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirk is a long dagger, and a dagger is kept in its fitted scabbard or case.

clue.text: Supply iron and get new gas

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, it means bendily, so the letters are flexed into another shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An instruction to provide some iron and obtain a fresh gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a verb meaning provide; it is the adverb from supple, rhyming with simply.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogen is the colourless element making up most of the air, an example of a gas.

clue.text: Apart from oars, ignore the odd parts below

indicators.note: skipping the first, third and so on keeps only the even-placed letters

blocks.note: second and fourth letters
under is a synonym of below

explanation.surface: Leaving the oars aside, don't bother with the odd bits below deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apart from' reads as a single phrase meaning except, but 'Apart' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn asunder means pulled into separate pieces, so the adverb matches apart.

clue.text: Negotiate most of recent diet changes

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its final letter
to change letters is to rearrange their order

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone bargains over the latest changes to their diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes' looks like a noun in the surface but works as the verb stirring the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To intercede is to step in and mediate between parties, much as a negotiator does.

clue.text: Like an anorak on Debra – dry on a regular basis

indicators.note: at regular intervals means taking every second letter

blocks.note: even-placed letters of the run

explanation.surface: Debra wears an anorak to stay dry, reliably, every time.
explanation.walkthrough: An anorak is a hooded waterproof jacket, but in British slang it is an obsessive enthusiast, like a trainspotter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang an anorak is an obsessive hobbyist, so being like one is geeky and uncool.

clue.text: Leading dance in hospital department

blocks.note: a prom is a formal school dance
taken as written
Ear, Nose and Throat, a hospital department

explanation.surface: Someone leads a dance held on a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one piece inside another, but it is just the letters IN, placed in line.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading figure is important and well known, which prominent also means.

clue.text: Perfect golf club softly scratched

indicators.note: a scratched runner is withdrawn, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: the club used on the green
p, piano, is the musical direction for softly

explanation.surface: A perfect golf club that got scratched gently.
explanation.walkthrough: PUTTER without P is UTTER. 'Perfect' is the adjective as in a perfect stranger.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter and perfect both mean complete or absolute, as in an utter fool or perfect idiot.

clue.text: English seat is possibly most comfortable

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several arrangements the letters could take

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for English
the two words rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone claims an English seat may be the comfiest one going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat is' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Easiest is the superlative of easy, meaning most relaxed and least troubled.

clue.text: Well-behaved soldier

blocks.note: neat and disciplined, as a well-run queue or tidy room
an army private assigned to attend an officer or carry messages

explanation.surface: A soldier who follows the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words seem to describe one soldier, but each is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly means disciplined and tidy, and as a noun names an attendant soldier or hospital porter.

clue.text: In report, mentions tourist attractions

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: to cite is to mention or quote

explanation.surface: A written report name-checks the local tourist attractions.
explanation.walkthrough: CITES and SIGHTS sound the same; the definition is at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The sights of a city are its notable places that visitors go to see.

clue.text: Christian maybe willing to receive the setter’s news

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: game for anything means willing
the setter is I, so the setter has is I have
N for new, twice over for the plural

explanation.surface: A willing Christian, perhaps, taking in the setter's news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' is a first name here, not a believer. 'The setter's' stands for the setter has, I'VE; 'news' is read as two lots of new.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian is one example of a first name, the personal name chosen at birth or baptism.

clue.text: Gathers information from Edward about underwear

indicators.note: turned about means turned round to face the other way

blocks.note: the short form of Edward
briefs are short underpants

explanation.surface: Someone learns things from Edward on the subject of his underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning, but it turns ED round.
explanation.definitionFit: To debrief someone is to question them after a mission to collect what they learned.

clue.text: It’s of benefit if you have a flat belly

definitions.text: It’s of benefit if you have a flat belly

blocks.clueFragment: It’s of benefit if you have a flat belly
blocks.note: surface reading: a toned, flat stomach is good for your health
setter's reading: a flat is a punctured wheel, so the extra one in the boot helps; and the thing itself is a roll of belly fat

explanation.walkthrough: Flat is a puncture, not toned; the answer is also slang for a paunch, the very opposite of a flat belly.
explanation.definitionFit: The extra wheel carried in a car saves the day after a puncture, and the phrase also means a paunch.

clue.text: Dreadful leaders in House of Representatives make fun of the French

indicators.note: leaders are the ones at the front, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: initial letters of the three words
to rib someone is to tease them
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Awful leaders in Congress mock the French.
explanation.walkthrough: HOR, RIB and LE run straight together.
explanation.definitionFit: Horrible and dreadful are close synonyms for something very bad or unpleasant.

clue.text: Class conflict

blocks.note: a ranked grouping, as a football league tier
disagreement that splits people

explanation.walkthrough: The pair reads as class war, but each word defines the answer separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A division is a ranked grouping or category, and also a split or disagreement between parties.

clue.text: Boss went missing with trainee

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: a boss is a raised knob or stud on a surface
taken as written
standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: The boss disappeared along with the apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went missing' looks like one phrase, but 'missing with' tells you to lose W from WENT. A boss here is an ornamental knob, not a manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A student is a learner being taught a trade or subject, just as a trainee is.

clue.text: Snaps out of it?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone recovers from a mood
setter's reading: snaps are photographs, and they come out of this device

explanation.walkthrough: 'Snaps out of it' is the idiom for shaking off a bad mood; read literally it means photographs emerging from something.
explanation.definitionFit: Snapshots are the pictures produced by the device used to take photographs.

clue.text: Article promises no advanced solutions

indicators.note: no here means without, so letters are left out

blocks.note: the indefinite article
to swear is to vow or promise
standard abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece that pledges no advanced remedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced' looks like a describing word for the solutions, but it is just the letter A struck out of the promises.
explanation.definitionFit: The answers to a puzzle are its solutions, the results that resolve each question.

clue.text: Ways England cricketer’s caught

indicators.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it, so this is about sound

blocks.note: Joe Root, England batsman and former captain, plus the possessive

explanation.surface: An England cricketer is dismissed caught in some fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like a cricket dismissal, but it means heard. In British speech the word is said to rhyme with boots; Joe Root is England's top Test run scorer.
explanation.definitionFit: Routes are paths or courses taken to get somewhere, much as ways are.

clue.text: Best cur one trained? Without question

indicators.note: something trained has been shaped and reworked, so the letters are reordered
in the old sense without means outside, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: the six letters rearranged
standard abbreviation for question

explanation.surface: Is the best dog the one that's been trained? Undoubtedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without question' reads as the idiom meaning certainly, but 'Without' means outside, wrapping round Q.
explanation.definitionFit: To best an opponent is to beat or overcome them, the verb sense of defeat.

clue.text: Hold cold fish

blocks.note: C for cold, as marked on taps
a ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold cold fish' reads like instructions for storing seafood; the verb is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling is to grip tightly and refuse to let go, keeping a firm grasp.

clue.text: Watch old boy in the military

blocks.note: a former pupil of a school
to be in the forces is to serve

explanation.surface: Someone keeps an eye on an old soldier in the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction, but the whole phrase is a verb for being a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe is to look at closely and take note, a synonym of the verb watch.

clue.text: Some stuck up colonel fires gun

indicators.note: some of the text means only a part of the letters is used
in a down clue, sent upward means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A snooty colonel shoots his gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up' reads as snobbish, but it flips the run of letters in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a long-barrelled firearm fired from the shoulder, one kind of gun.

clue.text: Picture this writer’s anger after finally getting dismissed

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of a word
whatever is dismissed is sent away, so it is removed

blocks.note: the writer says I am, contracted
rage is fury
last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Imagine the setter's fury at finally being sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' looks like an ordering word, but only its last letter is used, and that R is struck from RAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a representation such as a photograph or painting, a synonym for picture.

clue.text: Stroke goat, perhaps, then step on it

blocks.note: a goat is an example of an animal that butts
step on it means hurry, and to fly is to rush

explanation.surface: Pat a goat, then put your foot down and go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' looks like petting, but it is a swimming style; the goat is defined by example as something that butts.
explanation.definitionFit: The butterfly is a swimming style with both arms swung over together, one of the four competitive strokes.

clue.text: Harry near guests lacking upper-class grandeur

indicators.note: to harry is to harass and disturb, so the letters are thrown about
lacking something means going without it, so letters are removed

blocks.note: the two words, minus one letter
U is the old label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: Prince Harry, among guests, lacks posh splendour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' reads as the prince, but it is a verb meaning harass that stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandeur is magnificence or eminence, the quality of being great.

clue.text: Vegetable marrows we’d eaten, though not all

indicators.note: not all of the words are used, only a part of their letters

blocks.note: letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: We ate marrows, though not every one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The marrows look like the vegetable in question; the answer spans the words instead. A swede is the British name for a rutabaga.
explanation.definitionFit: The swede is a large yellow-fleshed root, known in America as a rutabaga.
